output:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Monnier, thank you for waiting. I know it has been a long night. You are your uncle's nephew, and his heir, I understand?

FÉLIX: That is what the lawyers will say, Inspector, though my uncle never said it to me. My father was Jules, his younger brother. My father died in 1889, and after that my uncle looked after me. I know he thought it was his duty, and I know I did not make it easy for him.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the dinner.

FÉLIX: My aunt had cooked a goose, and it was very good. Everybody came, as they do every year. Then, when the temple bell struck nine, my uncle asked us all to take out our watches, as he always does. He likes to tell you what is wrong with yours. He is usually right, which is the trouble with him.

MATTHEY: And your watch?

FÉLIX: Mine is my father's silver watch. I carry it. I have never let anyone regulate it, not my uncle, not anyone, and he knew that. When the temple struck nine my watch showed twenty minutes to nine. My uncle made a scene about it in front of everyone. He said a man who could not keep his father's watch in order could not be trusted with anything else. He laughed, and I wished very much that I had stayed in bed.

MATTHEY: What did you do after dinner?

FÉLIX: I went up to the library. I wanted to be away from the table, and from my uncle's face. I stayed there alone. I had brandy, and I will not pretend I did not.

MATTHEY: Did you look at your watch while you were there?

FÉLIX: When the temple struck ten my watch showed twenty to ten. I remember, because I thought, there, another hour gone and nothing decided.

MATTHEY: Tell me what you heard.

FÉLIX: My aunt was playing the piano downstairs. Chopin, I think. She plays Chopin when she is unhappy, though she would never say so. At eighteen minutes past ten by my watch I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. Then I heard my uncle's repeater sounding. I know that sound from my whole life. Ten slow deep notes. I counted those. Then some doubled notes, and then quick high ones, which I did not count. I think I did not want to know what they meant.

MATTHEY: Had you heard anything before the thump?

FÉLIX: Yes. At a quarter past ten by my watch someone went quickly up the stairs, past the library door. I heard it. Then at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch someone came quickly down. I did not see who. The door was shut.

MATTHEY: Did anyone come to the library?

FÉLIX: Bastien Girard. He came in at thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch, and we sat together there until the temple struck eleven. I suppose he wanted to talk about the repeater, since that was what he and my uncle had been quarrelling over, the price of it. I do not like him, Inspector, but I did not want to be alone.

MATTHEY: You owe money, I think.

FÉLIX: Some of it to Girard, yes. Not a great deal, but enough to make me a fool at the table. My uncle knew. He knew everything about me that was worth knowing and a good deal that was not.

MATTHEY: What did the repeater mean to him?

FÉLIX: Everything. He never let anyone see it until it was finished. He said my father would have understood it, and he said it to me as a reproach, which was his way.

MATTHEY: Did he ever touch your father's watch?

FÉLIX: He wanted to. He never got the chance.

MATTHEY: I understand you are afraid.

FÉLIX: I am, Inspector. I was alone in the library, directly under the atelier. Anyone who asks will see that, and I would see it too, if I were you.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Monsieur Monnier. Please do not leave the town.
